Disease Outbreak Hits Gas & Water Utilities Workforce in India, GAIL India Ltd Among Firms Affected

New Delhi, June 14 – A disease outbreak has affected workers at several Gas & Water Utilities sites across India, leading to operational disruptions and concerns over staff safety, industry officials said on Friday. GAIL India Ltd is among the companies reporting cases of illness, as authorities work to contain the spread and maintain essential services.

The outbreak, identified as an acute viral gastroenteritis, was first detected earlier this week at a major gas processing facility in western India. Since then, cases have been reported at multiple sites operated by both private and state-run utilities. Industry sources estimate that more than 220 workers across at least five sites have shown symptoms including severe vomiting, diarrhea and fever, resulting in significant absenteeism.

“Employee health and safety is our top priority. We have implemented additional sanitation and screening measures at all affected facilities,” a spokesperson for GAIL India Ltd said. “Operations have been adjusted to ensure continuity, but some delays and temporary reductions in output are occurring as a result of staffing shortages.”

Industry union representatives confirmed that several workers have been hospitalized, though most cases are reported as mild to moderate. “We are urging all companies to provide immediate medical care and paid leave for affected staff,” said Rajesh Kumar, General Secretary of the All India Gas & Water Employees Union. “There is anxiety among the workforce, especially those on shifts at larger processing plants.”

State health officials in Gujarat and Maharashtra, where the largest clusters have been reported, said teams have been dispatched to investigate the source of the outbreak and provide on-site medical support. Preliminary findings suggest contamination of drinking water at certain facilities may be a contributing factor, though a full investigation is ongoing.

Industry analysts say the outbreak could continue to impact staffing and output at gas and water processing plants if not contained swiftly. “These utilities run with minimum required personnel for safety and compliance. Extended absences can slow maintenance and processing schedules,” said Neha Verma, an independent energy sector analyst.

As of Friday afternoon, companies reported that contingency plans were in place and that critical operations remain functional. However, officials warned that the situation remains fluid, with further updates expected as health authorities complete their investigations.
